title: Three Hundred Thousand Savings Books
book: The Wages of Destruction: The Making and Breaking of the Nazi Economy
author: Adam Tooze
wiifm: Every book so far this week has explained a collapse through politics, networks or decisions. This one goes under all of that to the ledger, and argues that the Third Reich's trajectory was set by arithmetic its leadership partly understood and could not escape. The through-line is a savings stamp book that 336,638 ordinary Germans paid into for a car that was never going to exist. By the end you will have a habit worth more than the history: comparing balance sheets before comparing tactics.

b: On 1 August 1938 the German Labour Front launched a savings scheme. For a minimum of five Reichsmarks a week, bought as stamps and stuck into a book, an ordinary German worker could save towards a car, the Strength-Through-Joy car, priced politically at 990 Reichsmarks, later known to the world as the Volkswagen Beetle. When the book was full you had a claim on a vehicle.
It was the most popular consumer promise the regime ever made. 336,638 people paid in, hundreds of millions of marks of ordinary people's spare cash, lent interest-free to the state.

Not one of them received a car. The factory at Fallersleben built 630 saloons, which went to the Nazi elite. Everything else it produced was military: wings and wooden drop tanks for the Luftwaffe, 37,320 Kübelwagen utility vehicles from August 1940, 14,276 amphibians, 221,505 field ovens, and from 1943 components for the V1.

Hold that image, because Adam Tooze's eight hundred pages are an extended version of it. His subject is not the ideology of the Third Reich, which is well covered elsewhere. It is the arithmetic underneath, and his central claim, startling in 2006 and now close to orthodoxy, is that Nazi Germany was not an economic colossus that overreached. It was a middle-income country that knew it was running out of time.
ch.cap: Savings stamps fill books for a car never delivered

ch.h: An Englishman who learned to count Germany
b: The man who did the counting has a story that explains why he counted. Adam Tooze was born in London in 1967 and spent much of his childhood in West Germany, in Heidelberg, where his father, a molecular biologist, worked. He grew up between two languages and two national memories, in a country that was rich, orderly and very conscious of what had happened there a generation before.

He read economics at King's College, Cambridge, and then went to study at the Free University in Berlin. He arrived in 1989 and was in the city that November when the Wall came down, watching an economic system dissolve in a matter of weeks because its accounts no longer worked. His doctorate, at the London School of Economics, was not about battles or ideology at all. It was about statistics: how the German state learned to measure its own economy between 1900 and 1945.

That choice is the key to the book. Tooze knew the numbers of the Third Reich not as decoration but as artefacts, made by particular officials for particular purposes, which meant he could also tell when they were being used to flatter. He published The Wages of Destruction in 2006 while teaching at Cambridge, it won the Wolfson History Prize, and he went on to Yale and then Columbia, writing about the aftermath of the First World War and the financial crash of 2008 with the same opening question: what could each party actually pay for?
ch.cap: Tooze watches the Berlin Wall open, November 1989

ch.h: The poverty at the heart of the Reich
b: Start with the thing nobody expects. In the 1930s Germany was a middle-income European economy with world-class engineering in a handful of sectors and very ordinary living standards everywhere else. Large parts of agriculture were still worked by hand and horse. Most households had no car, no refrigerator, no telephone.

Tooze pushes this hard, at points suggesting German living standards were around a quarter of American levels, and this is the place to be careful, because the figure is contested. Angus Maddison's widely used estimates put German income per head at roughly seventy per cent of the American level in the same period. Those two numbers cannot both be right, and the honest position is that Tooze's broad point about relative backwardness survives even on the more conservative figure, while his most dramatic statements of it do not.

Remember, too, where the regime began. When Hitler became chancellor in January 1933, roughly six million Germans were registered as unemployed. The recovery that followed was real, and it was popular, but much of it was built on public works and, increasingly, on arms orders, not on a flood of new goods for households to buy.

Why does it matter? Because it inverts the standard picture. Aggression in 1939 reads naturally as the behaviour of a state that felt strong. Tooze's reading is the opposite: it was the behaviour of a state that believed its window was closing, and that the gap between itself and the Anglo-American world was widening rather than narrowing.
ch.cap: Jobless men queue while horses still pull the ploughs

b: Tooze argues that Hitler's strategic thinking was organised around the United States, not Britain, not France, not in the first instance even the Soviet Union.

America was the demonstration case: a continental state with vast resources and an enormous internal market delivering mass prosperity to ordinary people. That was precisely what the Nazi regime had promised and could not supply, as 336,638 empty savings books demonstrated. In the unpublished sequel to Mein Kampf, written in 1928, Hitler set out the conclusion plainly, that without additional living space, no social policy could ultimately succeed.

Follow the logic and the war in the east stops being an ideological add-on and becomes the economic programme. If German living standards cannot be raised inside German borders, and the American model requires continental scale, then the territory must be acquired. The racial ideology supplied the justification for who would be removed. The arithmetic supplied the reason for needing the land at all.
This is the uncomfortable gift of the book: it refuses to let you treat the regime's crimes as separate from its economics.
ch.cap: A dream of American plenty fills a Berlin window

b: The rearmament spending was real and enormous. Of the increase in German output between 1935 and 1938, military spending accounted for roughly forty-seven per cent, around sixty-seven per cent including associated investment, against about twenty-five per cent for personal consumption.

And it did not work, because Germany had to pay the outside world in a currency it did not have. Rearmament needed imported iron ore, rubber, oil, copper, tungsten, bauxite and fats. Exports had to earn the foreign exchange to buy them, and German exports were uncompetitive. So the regime improvised: an industrial levy that raised seven hundred million Reichsmarks in its first year, funding an average export subsidy approaching thirty per cent by late 1935, in effect a secret half-devaluation of its own currency, paid for by domestic industry.

By early 1939 it was visibly breaking down. The financial imbalance was disrupting the armaments programmes themselves, and the procurement crisis of that summer was not a plan but a scramble, with army, navy and Luftwaffe bidding for steel allocations that did not exist.
The structural point is portable and brutal. You can create money. You cannot create the physical input you buy from somebody else, in their currency, on their terms.
ch.cap: Printed marks pile up; oil and ore stay offshore

b: How do you pay for rearmament you cannot afford without anybody noticing? The man who answered was Hjalmar Schacht, president of the Reichsbank from 1933 and Economics Minister from 1934. His device was the Mefo bill. Arms contractors were paid in bills drawn on a shell company with a deliberately dull name, the Metallurgical Research Company, which the Reichsbank stood ready to cash. The spending never appeared in the budget. By 1938 something like twelve billion Reichsmarks had been raised this way.

Schacht also built the New Plan of 1934, a system of import licences and bilateral trade deals, many of them with south-eastern Europe and Latin America, designed to ration foreign currency to whatever the regime thought most important. It bought time. It did not solve the underlying problem, and by 1936 Schacht was arguing for rearmament to slow down.

Hitler went the other way. In August 1936 he wrote a memorandum demanding that within four years the army be ready for action and the economy fit for war, and he gave Hermann Göring a Four Year Plan to deliver it. Its centrepiece was substitution: oil made from coal, synthetic rubber, low-grade German iron ore. These processes worked, at a price. They swallowed enormous amounts of steel, labour and capital to make at home what could have been imported far more cheaply, if Germany had had the currency.

Schacht left the Economics Ministry in 1937. Tooze reads the whole episode as a choice made with open eyes: the regime understood that self-sufficiency was slow and expensive, and accepted it because the alternative was to depend on the very powers it intended to fight.
ch.cap: Coal goes in, costly synthetic oil comes out

b: Everyone knows how France fell in 1940: German armoured superiority and a revolutionary doctrine the Allies could not match. Now the numbers.

Germany attacked in the west in May 1940 with ninety-three divisions, of which just nine were Panzer divisions, fielding 2,439 tanks. France alone had 3,254 tanks; the Allies together had roughly 4,200 armoured vehicles. The Luftwaffe had 3,578 combat aircraft against about 4,469. German divisions moved largely on horses.

The word Blitzkrieg is barely German in origin, it was popularised by British wartime journalism and entrenched afterwards by the memoirs of German generals explaining their own brilliance. There was no coherent Blitzkrieg doctrine driving German weapons development; the armament programmes of 1936 and 1938 were aimed at a long war against Britain and France, and the 1940 campaign was won by concentrating armour at a single point, accepting enormous risk, and being right.

What actually won was a plan of breathtaking risk, associated with the staff officer Erich von Manstein. Instead of the expected drive through central Belgium, the main weight of German armour went through the wooded hills of the Ardennes, which the French had judged unsuited to tanks, crossed the river Meuse at Sedan on 13 May, and raced for the Channel coast. The Allied armies that had advanced into Belgium were cut off. Had the columns jammed in the Ardennes been caught from the air, the story might have been a German disaster.
Then the Reich spent five years attempting to repeat a gamble as if it were a method. That is the error the story is here to inoculate you against.
ch.cap: Tanks and horse wagons crawl through the Ardennes forest

ch.h: The ledger decides the long war
b: The second half of the book argues that the outcome was settled by resource arithmetic visible from 1941.

The decisive figure is American. The Lend-Lease appropriation of March 1941 was, on its own, worth roughly two years of total German domestic military spending. Before the United States had fired a shot, its legislature had committed to the Allied side a sum Germany could not match by any means available to it.

Seen this way, the invasion of the Soviet Union on 22 June 1941 was partly a race against that arithmetic. In Tooze's account, the regime hoped to seize the grain of Ukraine and the oil of the Caucasus quickly enough to build a continental economy before American production reached the battlefield. When the attack stalled outside Moscow that December, and Germany declared war on the United States days later, the race was effectively lost.

This is where Tooze parts company with the older account, associated with Richard Overy, in which German armaments were mismanaged until Albert Speer arrived and produced a miracle in 1942 to 1944 that Allied bombing then curtailed. Tooze gives Speer much less credit: a good deal of the increase was already in train before him, some of the reported gains were statistical artefacts of how output was counted, and the ceiling was set by coal, steel and labour rather than by organisation.

Speer himself, Hitler's architect, became armaments minister in February 1942 after his predecessor, Fritz Todt, was killed in a plane crash. He was a gifted organiser and an even more gifted publicist, and much of the legend of his miracle was written by Speer, in his memoirs, after the war.

The transferable discipline is simple and widely ignored. In any long contest, compare balance sheets before comparing tactics, and decline the contests you cannot fund to completion. Brilliance is a way of winning a short engagement. It is not a way of winning an attritional one.
ch.cap: American output lines climb far above Germany's

b: So the Reich did what states under resource pressure have always done, and Tooze costs it out without flinching. Occupied Europe was stripped. In 1942 and 1943, more than a fifth of Germany's grain, a quarter of its fats and close to thirty per cent of its meat came from occupied territories, and millions of foreign workers were brought into German industry, many of them by force.

And the yield fell every year. Confiscation destroyed the incentive to produce, so output in the occupied countries declined. Coerced labour is unproductive labour. The more the Reich took, the less there was to take, and the apparatus required to keep taking it consumed more of what it extracted.

His most disturbing chapters follow this logic into the east, where the economic plans were murderous on their own terms before any separate decision about extermination: Generalplan Ost envisaged displacing tens of millions of people, and the Hunger Plan of 1941 assumed that feeding the German army and population meant starvation for the populations of occupied Soviet territory.

Tooze is equally clear about where the arithmetic stops explaining anything. As labour ran short from 1942, some officials argued for keeping Jewish workers alive in war production. They mostly lost. In the murder of the Jews of Europe, ideology overrode the regime's own economic calculations again and again, and Tooze refuses to let economic history make the genocide look like a rational policy.
The general principle, at an infinitely smaller scale, holds wherever you squeeze a counterparty: it works once, and then it works less, and the cost of enforcement rises while the yield falls.
ch.cap: Grain trains leave occupied fields that yield less each year

b: Read him with three caveats, because this is a thesis book as well as an archival one.

First, originality. The pre-war chapters restate, in much greater detail, work by Avraham Barkai and Werner Abelshauser, and Barkai had already advanced a version of the land-hunger argument. The book's framing implies more novelty than the historiography supports.

Second, the living-standards estimates. Tooze's figure of around a quarter of American levels clashes irreconcilably with Maddison's roughly seventy per cent, and his critics have pressed him hard on it. The qualitative claim about German backwardness holds; the most arresting numbers do not.

Third, determinism. Tooze is sometimes read as implying that the squeeze made 1939 necessary. The counter-case is that Hitler had choices, took them for ideological reasons, and would probably have taken them in a stronger economy too. Tooze's own position is more careful than his summarisers', but the question of how far economics drove the decision for war remains genuinely open.

What survives all three is the method, and it is the reason the book closes this part of the week: before you explain any outcome with strategy, culture or will, establish what the party could physically afford.
ch.cap: Historians argue: a quarter of American wealth, or seventy?

Reorganisation cannot beat a materials ceiling

Tooze strips much of the credit from Speer's armaments miracle: the limit was coal, steel and labour, not management. Before restructuring anything, check whether the constraint is organisational at all.

What in Tooze's own background shaped how he read the Reich's numbers?

He grew up partly in Heidelberg, was in Berlin when the Wall fell in 1989, and wrote his doctorate on the history of German economic statistics. That made him treat official figures as things made for a purpose, and able to tell when they flattered the regime.

stories: Five marks a week for a Beetle

On 1 August 1938 the Nazi Labour Front made ordinary Germans an offer. Buy savings stamps, at least five Reichsmarks a week, stick them in a book, and when it was full you had a claim on a car: the Strength-Through-Joy car, priced at 990 Reichsmarks, later known as the Volkswagen Beetle. It was the regime's most popular promise. 336,638 people paid in, lending the state their spare cash interest-free. Not one saver received a car. The factory built 630 saloons for the Nazi elite, then turned to Kübelwagen, field ovens and parts for flying bombs. Adam Tooze's whole book is that savings stamp book, scaled up to a country.
The company with the dull name

How do you pay for rearmament you cannot afford without anyone noticing? Hjalmar Schacht, president of the Reichsbank, had an answer. Arms makers were paid not in cash but in bills drawn on a shell company with a deliberately boring name, the Metallurgical Research Company, known as Mefo. The Reichsbank stood ready to cash the bills, so contractors were content, and the spending never appeared in the budget. By 1938 something like twelve billion Reichsmarks had been raised this way. It bought time, not solvency. By 1936 Schacht himself was arguing for rearmament to slow down, and in 1937 he left the Economics Ministry.

Ask most people why France fell in 1940 and they will say German tanks. Now the numbers. Germany attacked with 2,439 tanks. France alone had 3,254. The Allies had more combat aircraft too, and most German divisions moved on horses. What won was a gamble: sending the armour through the wooded Ardennes, which the French thought unsuitable for tanks, across the Meuse at Sedan on 13 May and on to the Channel. Had the columns jammed in the forest been caught from the air, it might have been a German disaster. Even the word Blitzkrieg was popularised by British journalists rather than German doctrine. Germany then spent five years trying to repeat a gamble as if it were a method.
biz: Audit the promises in your adverts

The Volkswagen savers were sold something the factory was never going to make. A broker's version is smaller but real: promises in ads, landing pages and WhatsApp templates that your capacity cannot back up, such as a call within the hour or a quick decision. This week, list every promise made to customers across HomeownersLoan, Apply4Loan and Debt Support Direct. Beside each, write the measured reality, such as your actual median time to first contact. Anything you cannot reliably deliver comes out or gets fixed, because under Consumer Duty and the financial promotion rules a promise you cannot keep is a misleading one.
Do not fight a war you cannot fund

Tooze's lesson is to compare balance sheets before tactics. On Google and Bing, the broadest secured-loan searches are fought over by firms with budgets far larger than yours, and clever ad copy will not outlast them. Put your money where you can fund the contest to completion: narrower searches that match what you genuinely do well, and SEO content that keeps earning after the spend stops. Judge every channel by cost per completed loan, not cost per click or per enquiry. If a channel only looks good before completions are counted, it is winning a short engagement in a long war.
connects: Smith's case that nations grow rich through trade rather than self-sufficiency is the mirror image of the Nazi drive for autarky, which spent fortunes making at home what could have been bought far more cheaply abroad.
The Kelly principle of never staking more than your edge justifies is exactly what the Reich ignored when it treated the lucky gamble of 1940 as a repeatable method.

The Ardennes thrust of 1940 is the classic case of Liddell Hart's indirect approach, and Tooze's doubts about the Blitzkrieg legend are doubts about a story Liddell Hart and the German generals' memoirs helped to build.
recap:
In the summer of nineteen thirty-eight, the Nazi regime offered ordinary Germans a dream. Save five marks a week in a little stamp book, and one day you would own a car of your own, the car that became the Volkswagen Beetle. Three hundred and thirty-six thousand people paid in. None of them ever got a car. The factory made military vehicles instead, and the savings simply funded the state.

That savings book is the key to Adam Tooze's history of the Nazi economy. Tooze was born in London, grew up partly in Heidelberg, studied economics at Cambridge, and was a student in Berlin in nineteen eighty-nine when the Wall came down and a whole economic system dissolved because its accounts no longer worked. His doctorate was about how the German state measured its own economy, so he knew the Reich's numbers as objects made for a purpose, sometimes to flatter.

His first big idea is that Nazi Germany was not an economic giant. It was a middle-income country with brilliant engineering in a few places and ordinary living standards everywhere else, and its leaders believed their window was closing. His most dramatic figures for that poverty are disputed, but the broad point holds.

His second is that Hitler's eyes were on America. The United States showed what a continent-sized economy could deliver to ordinary people, and Hitler concluded that Germany needed land in the east to match it. The economics and the crimes cannot be separated.

His third is that you cannot print raw materials. Rearmament needed imported oil, ore and rubber, paid for in foreign currency Germany did not have. Secret bills hid the spending, and expensive home-made substitutes swallowed steel and labour.

His fourth is that the famous Blitzkrieg was a gamble, not a method. Germany beat France in nineteen forty with fewer tanks than its enemies, by risking everything on one thrust through the Ardennes, and then spent five years trying to repeat a stroke of luck.

And his fifth is that the ledger decides a long war. American Lend-Lease alone was worth about two years of German military spending, and squeezing occupied Europe produced less every year. Yet Tooze is clear that the murder of Europe's Jews defied even the regime's own economic logic.

Critics say he overstates his originality and some of his numbers. But his method survives them.

So remember this. Before you explain any contest by courage or genius, find out what each side could actually afford.
